title: Easy
description: Foundational software interview questions. Aim for clear, practical answers in 1-2 minutes.

questions.question: What is the difference between let, const, and var?
questions.sampleAnswer: I explain it in three parts: scope, reassignment, and hoisting behavior. var is function-scoped and can be redeclared, which often causes accidental overwrites. let and const are block-scoped, so they are safer inside loops and conditionals. let can be reassigned, while const cannot be reassigned after initialization. In modern code I default to const, use let when a value must change, and avoid var to reduce bugs.
hints: Start with scope, then assignment rules.
followUps: When would using let be better than const?
questions.voicePrompt: Tell me the difference between let, const, and var.

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.sampleAnswer: A closure happens when a function keeps access to variables from its outer scope even after that outer function has finished running. I use closures when I want private state, like counters or memoized functions, without exposing variables globally. For example, a function can return another function that increments an internal variable each call. That internal value stays available because the returned function closes over it.
followUps: How can closures cause memory issues?
questions.voicePrompt: What is a closure in JavaScript?

questions.question: Why use TypeScript instead of plain JavaScript?
questions.sampleAnswer: I use TypeScript because it catches many mistakes before runtime and improves maintainability. Static types make contracts between functions and components clear, which helps team collaboration. Editors also provide better autocomplete and refactoring support, so productivity goes up in larger codebases. I still run the app normally as JavaScript, but TypeScript gives me safer development feedback earlier.
hints: Mention runtime safety and team clarity.

questions.question: What is the difference between GET and POST requests?
questions.sampleAnswer: GET is mainly for reading data and should be safe and idempotent, meaning it does not change server state when repeated. POST is used to create or process data and can change server state. GET parameters are usually in the URL, while POST data is commonly in the request body. In practice, I use GET for fetching resources and POST when submitting forms or creating records.
followUps: When would you use PUT instead?

questions.question: What is the box model in CSS?
questions.sampleAnswer: The CSS box model describes how element size is calculated using content, padding, border, and margin. Content is the inner area where text or media appears. Padding adds space inside the border, border surrounds padding and content, and margin adds space outside the element. I usually set box-sizing to border-box so width and height include padding and border, which makes layouts easier to reason about.

questions.question: What is the purpose of reactive state in Vue?
questions.sampleAnswer: Reactive state lets the UI update automatically when data changes. Instead of manually touching the DOM, I change state and Vue tracks dependencies, then re-renders the needed parts efficiently. In Composition API I use ref for primitive values and reactive for object-like state. This model makes components predictable because rendering always reflects the current state.
followUps: When do you prefer computed over methods?
questions.voicePrompt: Why is reactive state important in Vue?

questions.question: What does git rebase do?
questions.sampleAnswer: git rebase reapplies my commits on top of another base commit so history looks linear. I use it to keep feature branches up to date with main before opening a pull request. The key difference from merge is that rebase rewrites commit hashes, while merge creates a merge commit. I avoid rebasing shared branches that others already pulled to prevent history conflicts.
followUps: When is merge a better choice?

questions.question: Name two quick ways to improve frontend performance.
questions.sampleAnswer: First, I reduce JavaScript bundle size through code splitting and removing unused dependencies, because smaller bundles load faster. Second, I optimize images by using modern formats and appropriate sizes for each viewport. I also watch caching headers and lazy-load non-critical UI sections, but if I only pick two, bundle size and image optimization usually give the fastest wins.
questions.voicePrompt: Give two fast frontend performance improvements.

questions.question: What is the difference between unit and integration tests?
questions.sampleAnswer: Unit tests verify a small piece of logic in isolation, usually a function or component behavior with dependencies mocked. Integration tests verify that multiple parts work together, such as a component with a real store or API layer mock server. I rely on unit tests for fast feedback and integration tests for confidence in actual user flows. A healthy project usually uses both.
hints: Tie each test type to confidence level.

questions.question: Why are semantic HTML elements important?
questions.sampleAnswer: Semantic HTML gives meaning to structure, which helps screen readers, keyboard navigation, and search engines understand content correctly. For example, using button for actions and nav for navigation is better than generic div elements with click handlers. It also reduces custom ARIA work because many semantics are built in. I treat semantic markup as the first step of accessible UI.

questions.question: What is event bubbling?
questions.sampleAnswer: Event bubbling means an event starts at the target element and then propagates upward through its parent elements. If I click a button inside a card, both button and card listeners can run unless propagation is stopped. I use this behavior for event delegation on lists to reduce many individual listeners. When needed, I call stopPropagation carefully to prevent unwanted parent handlers.

questions.question: What is JSON and why is it commonly used in APIs?
questions.sampleAnswer: JSON is a lightweight text format for structured data using key-value pairs and arrays. It is language-agnostic, easy for humans to read, and easy for machines to parse. Most web APIs use JSON because JavaScript handles it naturally and many backends support it out of the box. In practice it keeps request and response payloads simple and consistent.
followUps: When might XML still be used?
questions.voicePrompt: What is JSON and why use it in APIs?

questions.question: What is XSS and how do you prevent it?
questions.sampleAnswer: XSS, or cross-site scripting, happens when untrusted input is treated as executable script in the browser. I prevent it by escaping or sanitizing user-generated content, avoiding unsafe HTML injection, and using framework defaults that auto-escape templates. I also enforce a strong Content Security Policy to limit script sources. Prevention is best done in both frontend rendering and backend validation.
followUps: What is stored vs reflected XSS?
questions.voicePrompt: What is XSS and how do you avoid it?

questions.question: What does HTTP status code 404 mean?
questions.sampleAnswer: A 404 status means the server is reachable but the requested resource was not found at that path. It often happens with wrong URLs, deleted resources, or broken links. From a product side I provide a helpful fallback page and logging so we can trace where bad links come from. It is different from 500, which indicates a server error.
followUps: How do you handle 404 in SPAs?
questions.voicePrompt: What does a 404 status code tell you?

questions.question: How do you approach debugging a bug report?
questions.sampleAnswer: I start by reproducing the issue reliably and clarifying expected versus actual behavior. Then I isolate scope by checking logs, recent changes, and the smallest failing path. After identifying likely root causes, I test one hypothesis at a time instead of changing many things at once. Once fixed, I add a regression test and document the cause so the team can avoid repeating it.
followUps: What if you cannot reproduce locally?
